title: Anatomy and Physiology for Health and Social Care

format.summary: One written examination of 90 marks lasting 1 hour 30 minutes. Short- and long-answer questions and multiple-choice questions assessing understanding of the structure of human anatomy and the function of different body systems. Available in January and May/June.
tips: 90 marks in 90 minutes: roughly one mark per minute. Bank the 1-mark MCQs and 'state/define' items quickly so you have time for the 6–8 mark 'to what extent' questions.
Use precise anatomical vocabulary every time (e.g. 'alveoli', 'villi', 'vasodilation', 'beta cells of the islets of Langerhans') – vague words like 'stuff' or 'the tubes' cannot be credited.
For 'explain' questions, write in linked chains: structure → function → consequence ('because… which means… so…').
For data questions ('by how many', percentage change), show your working and include units; check whether the question wants a difference, a percentage or a percentage-point change.
For disorder questions, always name the body system, describe what normally happens, then what goes wrong and the effect on the person – and link to at least one other system.
'To what extent' needs a judgement: weigh the evidence and finish with a conclusion that answers the question directly.
If a question gives a case study or data, quote from it – the top band rewards applying knowledge to the detailed situation, not writing everything you know.

dDescriptor: Learners will be able to articulate arguments and views concisely and professionally to justify the conclusions they reach in relation to the functioning of different body systems. Learners will be able to show a depth of understanding of how the knowledge applies to detailed situations in relation to human anatomy and physiology. They will evaluate concepts to reach reasoned and valid judgements. They will draw on and show a synthesis of knowledge and understanding of the different body systems.

topics.title: How cells work
points: Describe the cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves the cell
Describe the nucleus: contains DNA and controls cell activities
Describe ribosomes: site of protein synthesis
Distinguish rough ER (has ribosomes, makes and transports proteins) from smooth ER (makes lipids and steroids)
Describe mitochondria: site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy (ATP)
Describe centrioles: organise spindle fibres during cell division
Describe lysosomes: contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and pathogens
Describe the Golgi apparatus: modifies, packages and secretes proteins
Link organelle numbers to cell function (e.g. muscle cells have many mitochondria)

topics.title: Characteristics of tissues
points: Simple epithelium: squamous (alveoli, capillaries), cuboidal (kidney tubules, glands), columnar (lining gut), ciliated (trachea, bronchi)
Compound epithelium: stratified (simple) and keratinised (skin) – protective layers
Connective tissue: blood, cartilage, bone, areolar, adipose – structure, location and function of each
Muscle tissue: striated/skeletal (voluntary), non-striated/smooth (involuntary, gut and vessel walls), cardiac (involuntary, does not fatigue)
Nervous tissue: neurones transmit impulses; neuroglia support and protect neurones
Link tissue structure to function (e.g. thin squamous cells give a short diffusion distance)

topics.title: The structure and function of body organs
points: Location, structure and function of the heart, lungs and brain
Location, structure and function of the stomach, liver, pancreas, duodenum, ileum and colon
Location, structure and function of the kidneys and bladder
Location, structure and function of the ovaries/testes and uterus
Structure and functions of the skin (protection, temperature regulation, sensation, vitamin D)

topics.title: Energy in the body
points: Energy transformations in the body: chemical, heat, sound, electrical, light
Role of energy in the body (movement, active transport, growth, maintaining temperature)
Anabolism: building larger molecules from smaller ones (requires energy)
Catabolism: breaking down larger molecules (releases energy)
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (in mitochondria)
Anaerobic respiration in humans: glucose → lactic acid + less energy; oxygen debt
Basal metabolic rate (BMR) and factors affecting it (age, sex, body size, activity, thyroxine)

topics.title: Human genetics
points: Key terms: gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, carrier
Use Punnett squares to work out probabilities of Mendelian inheritance
Autosomal recessive disorders: cystic fibrosis, PKU, sickle cell disease
Autosomal dominant disorder: Huntington's chorea
Chromosome disorder: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21)
Diagnostic testing: amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling (CVS) – when, how, risks and benefits

topics.title: Homeostatic mechanisms
points: Define homeostasis and the internal environment
Explain negative feedback (receptor, control centre, effector, return to set point)
Temperature: heat production and loss; roles of the hypothalamus and autonomic nervous system
Responses to heat and cold: vasodilation/vasoconstriction of arterioles, sweating, shivering
Surface area to volume ratio and heat loss (e.g. infants lose heat faster); fever
Blood glucose: roles of the pancreas, liver, insulin and glucagon
Fluid balance: water intake, output and loss; role of the kidneys and renal system
Failure of homeostasis: hypothermia and dehydration

topics.title: Cardiovascular system
points: Heart structure: chambers, valves, septum, major vessels
Cardiac cycle: atrial systole, ventricular systole, diastole
Heart rate and its regulation; stroke volume; cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume
Blood pressure (systolic/diastolic)
Blood vessels: arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins – structure related to function
Pulmonary and systemic circulation (double circulation)
Structure and function of blood: plasma, red cells, white cells, platelets
Disorders: coronary heart disease (CHD), stroke, anaemia, hypertension

topics.title: Respiratory system
points: Role of the nasal air passages (warming, moistening, filtering air)
Structure and function of the trachea, bronchi, bronchial tree, lungs and alveoli
Role of ciliated epithelial tissue and mucus
Respiratory muscles: intercostal muscles and diaphragm
Ventilation (inspiration/expiration) and its regulation
Gaseous exchange by diffusion at the alveoli
Disorders: smoking-related damage, asthma, COPD, pneumonia

topics.title: Skeletal system
points: Axial and appendicular skeleton
Types of bone: long, short, flat, irregular, sesamoid
Functions: support, protection, muscle attachment, blood cell production, mineral store
Ligaments and cartilage: structure and function
Locate the major bones named in the spec (cranium to metatarsals, vertebral column)
Joint classification: fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial; synovial joint structure
Movements: flexion, extension, circumduction, adduction, abduction, gliding
Disorders: fractures, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, increase in rickets

topics.title: Muscular system
points: Structure of striated (skeletal) muscle
Attachment: tendons and fascia
Types of contraction: isometric, concentric, eccentric
Antagonistic pairs: agonist, antagonist, synergist, fixator
Location and action of the major muscles named in the spec
Disorder: muscular dystrophy

topics.title: Digestive system
points: Alimentary canal: oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, ileum, colon
Accessory organs: liver, pancreas, salivary glands
Processes: ingestion, peristalsis, digestion, absorption, egestion
Enzymes: amylases, proteases, lipases – site of secretion and action
Role of microorganisms (gut bacteria) in the gut
Products of digestion and their uses; storage of excess fat and carbohydrate
Deamination of excess amino acids in the liver; urea removed by the kidneys
Absorption into blood and lacteals; role of villi and microvilli
Disorders: ulcers, hepatitis, coeliac disease

topics.title: Nervous system
points: CNS (brain and spinal cord): coordination of voluntary and involuntary activity
Peripheral nervous system: sensory and motor neurones
Sympathetic ('fight or flight') and parasympathetic ('rest and digest') divisions
Conduction of nerve impulses to and from the CNS (including the role of myelin and synapses)
Disorders: Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis (MS), dementia

topics.title: Endocrine system
points: Hypothalamus: controls the pituitary via releasing hormones; daily rhythms
Pituitary: growth, sex organ function, osmoregulation (ADH)
Thyroid: regulation of growth and metabolism; blood calcium regulation
Ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone) and testes (androgens, sperm production)
Pancreas: insulin and glucagon
Adrenal glands: adrenaline (fight or flight) and aldosterone (blood pressure)
Disorders: diabetes mellitus (type 1 and type 2), diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism

topics.title: Lymphatic and immune systems
points: Lymph: formed from tissue fluid and returned to the blood
Lymphatic vessels and lymphatic organs (formation and maturation of lymphocytes)
Immune response via T and B lymphocytes
Spleen: filtering blood and recycling parts of red blood cells
Disorders: Hodgkin's disease (lymphoma) and leukaemia

topics.title: Renal system
points: Kidneys: filter toxins from the blood; regulate water, salt balance and pH
Ureters carry urine to the bladder; bladder stores urine; urethra carries urine out
Disorders: urinary tract infections (UTIs) and renal failure

topics.title: Reproductive system
points: Female structures and functions: ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina, vulva
Male structures and functions: penis, urethra, scrotum, testes, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland
Disorders: endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, hydrocele, prostate cancer/BPH
Gamete production by meiosis
Conception: fertilisation to birth, cell division and chromosome behaviour
Foetal development through the trimesters and birth
Mitosis and DNA replication for growth
Factors affecting prenatal development: genetics, maternal age, diet, health, smoking, alcohol
Teratogens and their effects; congenital disorders: spina bifida, cerebral palsy, effects of rubella

topics.title: Medical research: how data is collected and used
points: Clinical trials: placebo, double-blind design and why they reduce bias
Epidemiological studies: patterns and causes of disease in populations
Mortality (deaths) and morbidity (illness) statistics
Data analysis: calculate differences, percentages and percentage change from tables and graphs
Use data to evaluate the efficacy of medical procedures and the effects of lifestyle choices

mcq.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
mcq.why: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing energy as ATP.

mcq.q: Which organelle modifies, packages and secretes proteins?
mcq.why: The Golgi apparatus processes proteins from the rough ER and packages them into vesicles for secretion.

mcq.q: Pancreatic cells secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes (which are proteins). Which organelle would you expect to find in large amounts in these cells?
mcq.why: Rough ER is studded with ribosomes, so it makes and transports large quantities of protein.

mcq.q: Which tissue lines the trachea and moves mucus away from the lungs?
mcq.why: Ciliated epithelium has cilia that beat to sweep mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat.

mcq.q: Why is simple squamous epithelium found lining the alveoli?
options: It is thick and protects against infection
It secretes mucus to trap dust
It contracts to push air out
It is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
mcq.why: Flat, single-layer cells give a very short diffusion pathway for oxygen and carbon dioxide.

mcq.q: Which type of muscle tissue is striated, involuntary and resistant to fatigue?
mcq.why: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but contracts involuntarily and continuously without tiring.

mcq.q: Which organ produces bile?
mcq.why: Bile is made in the liver; the gall bladder only stores it.

mcq.q: What is the main function of the ileum?
mcq.why: The ileum is lined with villi that absorb digested food into the blood and lacteals.

mcq.q: Which statement best describes anabolism?
options: Breaking down large molecules to release energy
Building larger molecules from smaller ones, using energy
mcq.why: Anabolic reactions build molecules (e.g. proteins from amino acids) and require energy; catabolism breaks them down.

mcq.q: During intense exercise, muscle cells respire anaerobically. What is produced?
mcq.why: In humans, anaerobic respiration converts glucose to lactic acid, releasing much less energy than aerobic respiration.

mcq.q: Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is best defined as:
options: the minimum energy needed to keep vital functions going at rest
the energy content of food eaten in a day
the rate at which food is digested
mcq.why: BMR is the energy needed at complete rest for functions such as breathing, circulation and maintaining body temperature.

mcq.q: Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder. Both parents are carriers. What is the probability that their child will have cystic fibrosis?
mcq.why: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff – one in four (25%) is ff and affected.

mcq.q: Huntington's chorea is caused by a dominant allele. One parent is heterozygous and the other is unaffected. What is the probability their child inherits the condition?
mcq.why: Hh × hh gives Hh, Hh, hh, hh – half the offspring inherit the dominant allele.

mcq.q: What causes Down's syndrome?
options: A deletion on the X chromosome
mcq.why: Down's syndrome is a chromosome disorder (trisomy 21), usually caused by non-disjunction during meiosis.

mcq.q: Which diagnostic test samples cells from the placenta and can be carried out earlier in pregnancy than amniocentesis?
mcq.why: CVS takes a small sample of placental tissue (chorionic villi) and is usually done earlier in pregnancy than amniocentesis; both carry a small risk of miscarriage.

mcq.q: Which statement describes negative feedback?
options: It increases a change away from the normal level
It only uses nerves, never hormones
It reverses a change so a variable returns towards its set point
mcq.why: Negative feedback detects a deviation and triggers responses that bring the variable back towards normal.

mcq.q: When core body temperature rises, what happens to the arterioles supplying skin capillaries?
options: They vasodilate so more heat is lost from the skin
They vasoconstrict so less heat is lost
They have no role in temperature control
mcq.why: Vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface, increasing heat loss by radiation.

mcq.q: After a large meal, blood glucose rises. Which response restores normal levels?
options: Beta cells in the pancreas release insulin
mcq.why: Insulin causes cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert it to glycogen, lowering blood glucose.

mcq.q: Why do newborn babies lose heat more quickly than adults?
options: They have a larger surface area to volume ratio
mcq.why: A larger surface area relative to volume means more heat is lost through the skin.

mcq.q: Illustrative data: at rest, heart rate = 70 bpm and stroke volume = 70 ml. During exercise, heart rate = 140 bpm and stroke volume = 100 ml. By how many ml/min does cardiac output increase?
Which blood vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
mcq.why: The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

mcq.q: Which is a major long-term risk of untreated hypertension?
mcq.why: High blood pressure damages artery walls and increases the risk of stroke and CHD.

mcq.q: A person with iron-deficiency anaemia often feels tired and breathless because:
options: their blood has reduced capacity to carry oxygen
their white cell count is too high
their heart rate is too low
mcq.why: Less haemoglobin means less oxygen is delivered to tissues for aerobic respiration.

mcq.q: What happens during inspiration?
options: The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards
Thoracic volume decreases and pressure rises
The external intercostals relax and ribs move down
The diaphragm contracts and flattens and thoracic volume increases
mcq.why: Increased thoracic volume lowers pressure in the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in.

mcq.q: Which feature of alveoli makes gas exchange efficient?
options: A large surface area and a rich capillary network
mcq.why: A large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply maintain a steep concentration gradient for diffusion.

mcq.q: Illustrative data: a patient's peak flow is 300 L/min. Their predicted peak flow is 450 L/min. What percentage of their predicted value is this?
In emphysema (a form of COPD), why is gas exchange reduced?
options: The alveolar walls break down, reducing surface area
Red blood cells carry too much oxygen
mcq.why: Damaged alveoli merge into larger air spaces with less total surface area for diffusion.

mcq.q: The patella is an example of which type of bone?
mcq.why: Sesamoid bones develop within a tendon; the patella sits in the quadriceps tendon.

mcq.q: Moving the arm sideways away from the midline of the body is called:
mcq.why: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline; adduction brings it back towards the midline.

mcq.q: Why are post-menopausal women at higher risk of osteoporosis?
options: Falling oestrogen levels lead to loss of bone density
mcq.why: Oestrogen helps maintain bone density; after the menopause bone is lost faster than it is replaced.

mcq.q: During the lifting phase of a bicep curl, which muscle is the agonist?
mcq.why: The biceps brachii contracts to flex the elbow; the triceps is the antagonist and relaxes.

mcq.q: A muscle lengthening while still under tension (e.g. lowering a weight slowly) is which type of contraction?
mcq.why: Eccentric contraction: the muscle lengthens under tension to control the movement.

mcq.q: Which statement about muscular dystrophy is correct?
options: It is caused by a bacterial infection
It is a group of genetic conditions causing progressive muscle weakness
It is caused by lack of vitamin D
mcq.why: Muscular dystrophies are inherited conditions in which muscle fibres progressively weaken and break down.

mcq.q: Which enzyme group digests proteins into peptides and amino acids?
mcq.why: Proteases (e.g. pepsin in the stomach) break down proteins.

mcq.q: The products of fat digestion are mainly absorbed into which structures in the villi?
mcq.why: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into lacteals, part of the lymphatic system.

mcq.q: In coeliac disease, why might a person lose weight and become malnourished?
options: Gluten triggers an immune reaction that damages the villi, reducing absorption
The colon absorbs too much water
mcq.why: Flattened, damaged villi greatly reduce the surface area for absorption of nutrients.

mcq.q: Where does deamination of excess amino acids take place?
mcq.why: The liver removes the amino group, forming urea, which is carried in the blood to the kidneys for excretion.

mcq.q: Which is an effect of the parasympathetic nervous system?
options: Decreases heart rate and stimulates digestion
mcq.why: The parasympathetic system is 'rest and digest': it slows the heart and increases digestive activity.

mcq.q: Multiple sclerosis slows nerve impulse conduction because:
mcq.why: MS is an autoimmune condition that damages myelin, so impulses travel more slowly or are blocked.

mcq.q: Parkinson's disease is associated with:
options: loss of dopamine-producing neurones in the brain
mcq.why: Reduced dopamine causes tremor, rigidity and slow movement.

mcq.q: Which hormone from the adrenal glands helps regulate blood pressure?
mcq.why: Aldosterone increases sodium (and so water) reabsorption by the kidneys, raising blood volume and pressure.

mcq.q: A person passes very large volumes of dilute urine and is constantly thirsty, but their blood glucose is normal. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.why: Diabetes insipidus involves lack of ADH (or kidney insensitivity to it), so water is not reabsorbed; glucose is unaffected.

mcq.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of hypothyroidism?
options: Weight loss, feeling hot, rapid heart rate
Excess thirst and high blood glucose
Tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold
mcq.why: Low thyroxine reduces metabolic rate, causing fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance.

mcq.q: Which cells produce antibodies?
mcq.why: B cells produce antibodies; T cells help coordinate the response and destroy infected cells.

mcq.q: Why are urinary tract infections more common in females than males?
options: Females have a shorter urethra, so bacteria reach the bladder more easily
mcq.why: A shorter urethra close to the anus gives bacteria a shorter route to the bladder.

mcq.q: Where does fertilisation normally take place?
mcq.why: The egg is fertilised in the fallopian tube and the zygote then moves to the uterus to implant.

mcq.q: Which statement about meiosis is correct?
options: It produces two identical diploid cells
It is used for growth and repair
It produces four genetically different haploid gametes
mcq.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates variation; mitosis produces identical cells for growth.

mcq.q: Illustrative trial: 200 people took a new drug and 30 had a stroke; 200 people took a placebo and 50 had a stroke. By how many percentage points was the stroke rate lower in the drug group?
mcq.why: Drug: 30/200 = 15%; placebo: 50/200 = 25%; difference = 10 percentage points (a 40% relative reduction).

long.context: Amira, aged 17, eats a large bowl of pasta and a fizzy drink at lunchtime. Two hours later, her blood glucose has returned to normal.
long.q: Explain how negative feedback returns Amira's blood glucose to normal after her meal.
markingPoints: Carbohydrate is digested to glucose, which is absorbed so blood glucose rises above the set point
The rise is detected by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
Beta cells secrete insulin into the blood
Insulin increases glucose uptake by body cells (e.g. muscle) for respiration
Insulin stimulates the liver (and muscles) to convert glucose to glycogen for storage
Blood glucose falls back towards normal; as it returns, insulin secretion decreases (the response switches off – negative feedback)
If glucose fell too low, alpha cells would release glucagon to convert glycogen back to glucose
dHallmarks: Uses the full feedback loop language: stimulus → receptor → control centre → effector → response → return to set point
Names specific cells and organs (beta cells, islets of Langerhans, liver) rather than 'the body'
Explains why the response switches off, showing what makes it negative feedback
Applies to Amira's meal throughout
long.model: Amira's pasta is digested into glucose, which is absorbed in her ileum, so her blood glucose rises above its set point. This change is detected by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in her pancreas, which secrete insulin into the blood. Insulin makes body cells such as muscle cells take up more glucose for respiration and stimulates her liver to convert glucose into glycogen for storage. As a result, her blood glucose falls back towards normal. Because the level is now back at the set point, the beta cells reduce insulin secretion, so the correction stops – this is negative feedback, because the response reverses the original change. If her level then dropped too low, alpha cells would release glucagon so the liver converts glycogen back to glucose.

long.q: Explain the events of the cardiac cycle.
markingPoints: Diastole: heart muscle relaxes; atria fill with blood from the vena cava and pulmonary vein
Atrial systole: atria contract, pushing blood through the atrioventricular (tricuspid/bicuspid) valves into the ventricles
Ventricular systole: ventricles contract; AV valves close (preventing backflow) and blood is forced through the semilunar valves into the aorta and pulmonary artery
Semilunar valves close when ventricles relax, preventing backflow; the cycle repeats (around 0.8 s at rest)
dHallmarks: Correct sequence with named chambers, valves and vessels
Explains why valves open and close (pressure differences)
Links each stage to its purpose (one-way flow)
long.model: During diastole the heart muscle relaxes and blood flows into the atria from the vena cava (right) and pulmonary vein (left). In atrial systole the atria contract, raising pressure so blood is pushed through the tricuspid and bicuspid valves into the ventricles. In ventricular systole the ventricles contract; the rise in pressure shuts the atrioventricular valves to stop backflow and opens the semilunar valves, so blood is forced into the pulmonary artery and aorta. When the ventricles relax, pressure in them falls and the semilunar valves close, preventing blood flowing back, and the cycle begins again.

long.context: Jamal eats a cheese sandwich, which contains starch, protein and fat.
long.q: Explain the role of enzymes in the digestion and absorption of Jamal's sandwich.
markingPoints: Salivary amylase in the mouth begins breaking starch into maltose (sugars)
Pepsin (a protease) in the stomach breaks proteins into peptides; acid gives the optimum pH and kills bacteria
Pancreatic juice in the duodenum contains amylase, proteases (e.g. trypsin) and lipase
Bile from the liver emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
Lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Enzymes on the ileum lining complete digestion to glucose and amino acids
Glucose and amino acids are absorbed into blood capillaries in the villi; fatty acids and glycerol into lacteals
Villi and microvilli give a large surface area for absorption
dHallmarks: Matches each enzyme to its substrate, site of secretion and product
Explains (not just names) the role of bile and of villi
Follows the food through the alimentary canal in the correct order
Applies to the cheese sandwich components
long.model: Digestion of the bread's starch starts in the mouth, where salivary amylase breaks it into sugars such as maltose. In the stomach, pepsin, a protease, begins breaking the cheese's protein into peptides, working best in the acidic conditions produced there. In the duodenum, pancreatic juice adds more amylase, proteases and lipase. Bile from the liver emulsifies the cheese's fat into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase, which breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Enzymes in the ileum lining complete digestion to glucose and amino acids. These small molecules are absorbed by the villi: glucose and amino acids enter the blood capillaries, while fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteals. The villi and microvilli provide a very large surface area, so absorption is fast and efficient.

long.context: Priya touches a hot pan and pulls her hand away.
long.q: Explain how nerve impulses travel to and from the central nervous system to produce Priya's response.
markingPoints: Receptors in the skin detect the heat (stimulus) and generate an impulse
The impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the CNS (spinal cord)
In the CNS the impulse passes across synapses (via relay neurones) using neurotransmitter chemicals
The impulse travels along a motor neurone to the effector (muscle in the arm), which contracts to move the hand
Myelin sheath insulates neurones and speeds up conduction
dHallmarks: Correct pathway: receptor → sensory neurone → CNS → motor neurone → effector
Explains synaptic transmission and myelin, not just lists them
Links to the speed and protective purpose of the response
long.model: Heat receptors in Priya's skin detect the stimulus and generate electrical impulses. These travel along a sensory neurone to her spinal cord, part of the CNS. At synapses the impulse is passed on chemically by neurotransmitters, via a relay neurone, to a motor neurone. The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector – the muscles in her arm – which contract and pull her hand away. Because the neurones are myelinated, the impulse travels quickly, and because it is processed in the spinal cord it is very fast, protecting her from a burn.

long.q: Compare and contrast the structure and function of arteries and veins.
markingPoints: Similarity: both are blood vessels with three layers in their walls and carry blood around the body
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood back towards the heart
Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and maintain high pressure; veins have thinner walls
Veins have a wider lumen and valves to prevent backflow at low pressure; arteries (apart from the heart's exit) have no valves
Arteries usually carry oxygenated blood, veins deoxygenated (except pulmonary vessels)
dHallmarks: Gives at least one genuine similarity as well as differences
Each structural difference is linked to function (pressure)
Notes the pulmonary exception
long.model: Both arteries and veins are blood vessels with walls made of three layers, carrying blood as part of the double circulation. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, so they have thick, muscular and elastic walls and a narrow lumen. Veins return blood to the heart at low pressure, so they have thinner walls, a wider lumen and valves that prevent backflow. Most arteries carry oxygenated blood and most veins deoxygenated blood, but the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein are the exceptions.

long.context: Dennis, aged 58, was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes three years ago. He has high blood pressure, his feet tingle, a small cut on his foot is slow to heal and his GP has found protein in his urine.
long.q: To what extent does type 2 diabetes affect body systems other than the endocrine system? Refer to Dennis in your answer.
markingPoints: Type 2 diabetes: cells become resistant to insulin (and/or insufficient insulin), so blood glucose stays high – an endocrine/homeostatic failure
Cardiovascular: high glucose damages blood vessel walls, contributing to atherosclerosis, hypertension, CHD and stroke risk – Dennis has high blood pressure
Renal: damage to kidney blood vessels reduces filtration; protein in urine suggests kidney damage, which may progress to renal failure
Nervous: high glucose damages peripheral nerves (neuropathy) – Dennis's tingling feet
Circulation and immunity: reduced blood flow to extremities and impaired healing mean infections and slow-healing wounds – his cut
Sense organs/eyes: damage to small vessels in the retina can affect vision
Links between systems: e.g. kidney damage worsens blood pressure, which further damages vessels
Judgement: the effects are wide-ranging and interlinked, so diabetes is a multi-system disorder; the extent depends on how well blood glucose, weight and blood pressure are controlled
dHallmarks: Synthesises at least three systems and explains the mechanism (high glucose damaging vessels/nerves), not just lists effects
Uses every clue in the case (BP, tingling, slow healing, protein in urine)
Shows interrelationships between systems (e.g. renal–cardiovascular cycle)
Reaches a reasoned, qualified judgement answering 'to what extent'
long.model: Type 2 diabetes begins as an endocrine problem: Dennis's cells have become resistant to insulin, so his blood glucose remains high. However, the persistently high glucose damages blood vessels and nerves throughout the body, so its effects extend well beyond the endocrine system. In the cardiovascular system it contributes to damage and narrowing of arteries, which helps explain Dennis's high blood pressure and increases his risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. In the renal system, damage to the small blood vessels in the kidneys reduces filtration, so protein leaks into his urine – an early sign that could progress to renal failure. Raised blood pressure and kidney damage worsen each other, showing how the systems are interlinked. His tingling feet suggest peripheral neuropathy, where high glucose damages sensory neurones, so he may not notice injuries. Combined with poor circulation to his feet and weaker immune responses, this explains why his cut is slow to heal and could become infected. Overall, type 2 diabetes affects the cardiovascular, renal, nervous and immune systems to a large extent, making it a multi-system disorder; however, the extent of damage is not fixed, as good control of his blood glucose, blood pressure and weight could slow its progression.

long.context: Maureen, aged 67, smoked for 40 years and has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). She is breathless climbing stairs, has a persistent productive cough and her oxygen saturation is lower than normal.
long.q: To what extent can Maureen's symptoms be explained by changes to her respiratory system caused by COPD?
markingPoints: Smoking damages cilia and increases mucus production; mucus is not cleared, causing a productive cough and infection risk
Airways (bronchi/bronchioles) become inflamed and narrowed (chronic bronchitis), increasing resistance to airflow
Alveolar walls break down (emphysema), reducing surface area for gaseous exchange
Lungs lose elasticity, so air is trapped and expiration is difficult
Less oxygen diffuses into the blood, lowering oxygen saturation; less oxygen reaches muscles for aerobic respiration, causing breathlessness and fatigue on exertion
Judgement: most symptoms are explained by respiratory changes, but the heart also has to work harder (cardiovascular link) and age-related decline/deconditioning may contribute
dHallmarks: Links each symptom to a specific structural change
Uses diffusion/surface area reasoning to explain low oxygen saturation
Recognises other contributing factors before concluding
long.model: Most of Maureen's symptoms can be explained by COPD. Long-term smoking has damaged the cilia in her airways and increased mucus production, so mucus builds up and she has a persistent productive cough. Her bronchi and bronchioles are inflamed and narrowed, making it harder to move air in and out. In emphysema, alveolar walls break down, reducing the surface area available for gaseous exchange, and the lungs lose elasticity, so air is trapped. As a result, less oxygen diffuses into her blood, explaining her low oxygen saturation, and her muscles receive less oxygen for aerobic respiration, so she becomes breathless climbing stairs. However, not everything is respiratory: her heart must work harder to supply oxygen, and her age and reduced fitness may add to breathlessness. Overall, COPD explains her symptoms to a large extent, but other systems also contribute.

long.context: Illustrative (fictional) data. A double-blind trial tested a new blood pressure drug. 240 adults with hypertension were randomly allocated: 120 to the drug and 120 to an identical-looking placebo. Results after 12 weeks: Drug group – mean systolic BP at start 158 mmHg, at 12 weeks 142 mmHg; 18 people reported side effects; 6 dropped out. Placebo group – start 157 mmHg, at 12 weeks 154 mmHg; 9 people reported side effects; 4 dropped out.
long.q: (a) Deduce by how many mmHg the reduction in mean systolic blood pressure was greater in the drug group than in the placebo group. (2) (b) To what extent does this trial show that the drug is effective and should be used? (6)
markingPoints: (a) Drug reduction = 158 − 142 = 16 mmHg; placebo reduction = 157 − 154 = 3 mmHg
(a) Difference = 13 mmHg greater reduction in the drug group
Double-blind design means neither participants nor researchers knew who received the drug, reducing bias
Placebo controls for the placebo effect – the small placebo fall shows some improvement occurs anyway
Random allocation makes groups comparable (similar starting BP)
Reasonable sample size (240) but only 12 weeks – long-term effects and outcomes such as strokes are unknown
Side effects were twice as common with the drug (18 vs 9), which must be weighed against benefits
Mean values hide individual variation; dropouts may bias results; only adults with hypertension – may not generalise
Judgement: good evidence the drug lowers BP in the short term, but more, longer research is needed before wide use
dHallmarks: Correct calculation with units and working
Uses the data (starting BPs, side-effect counts, dropouts) rather than generic comments
Evaluates the design (double-blind, placebo, randomisation, duration, sample)
Balanced, qualified judgement linked to patient safety and efficacy
long.model: (a) The drug group fell by 158 − 142 = 16 mmHg and the placebo group by 157 − 154 = 3 mmHg, so the drug group's reduction was 13 mmHg greater. (b) The trial gives fairly strong evidence that the drug lowers blood pressure. It was double-blind, so neither participants nor researchers could influence results through their expectations, and the placebo group shows that only a small fall (3 mmHg) happens without the drug. Random allocation produced groups with very similar starting blood pressures, so the comparison is fair, and 240 participants is a reasonable sample. However, the trial lasted only 12 weeks, so we do not know whether the effect lasts or whether it actually prevents strokes or heart attacks. Side effects were reported by twice as many people on the drug (18 compared with 9), and some participants dropped out, which could bias the means. Overall, the drug appears effective in the short term, but larger, longer trials looking at side effects and long-term outcomes would be needed before recommending it widely.
